ComprehensionText:
I was lying in bed, reading, when I heard an odd scratching sound at the door.

I sighed. I put my book aside and went to open it. There was my little sister, Bonita, down on the ground on all fours. She looked up at me, opened her mouth and made a long, loud squeaking sound instead of saying my name, James.

I told her to go and bother someone else but she just stared. Then she scuttled past me and hid under my bed. She was amazingly quick!

I bent down to see where she was. She was hiding against the wall, in the darkness. I asked her to come out but she shook her head and squeaked again.

Now, you might think this is very strange behaviour, but there is a reason for it. You see, Bonita really wants a guinea pig but Mum says she can't have one. So Bonita says that if she can't have a guinea pig, then she'll pretend to be one until Mum says yes.

So that's what she was doing under my bed. The only way I could get her to come out was by offering her a carrot. I dangled it in the air, and she followed me (crawling, of course) out the door, down the hallway and back to her own room. Phew! This has been going for three days now. I hope Mum says yes to a guinea pig soon, because my little sister is driving me crazy!
QuestionText: Bonita is acting like a guinea pig because
AnswerA: she wants her brother to play with her.
AnswerB: she wants to persuade her mother to buy her a guinea pig.
AnswerC: she wants to avoid being punished by her mother.
AnswerD: she wants her mother to buy her a guinea pig.

By Mary Leister One summer morning, a young blackbird clung to a cattail stem near his nest. His mother had woven the nest from fresh grasses, but it was now brown and dry. It hung crookedly in a clump of cattails on the edge of a farm pond. The little brown bird held tightly to a stem and flapped his wings. On a nearby cattail, his father's yellow head glowed in the sun. Both parents clucked nervously as they watched their last baby learn to fly.

The little bird blinked his dark eyes and looked around. He saw a world of green plants and sparkling water. He fluffed up his feathers. Then he flapped his wings again and gave a little push with his feet against the cattail stem. All of a sudden, something really special happened—off he went flying through the air! He wobbled as he flew across the edge of the farm pond and looked for a place to land. His toes grabbed a long thin willow branch that hung out over the water. But the branch sagged under his weight. He slipped off the end of it and plopped down into the pond!

Now the little bird's parents hopped around the cattails and called to their baby. But there was nothing they could do to help him. Then something special happened again. The little bird began to swim! He dipped his wing tips low into the water. When he pushed back FCAT 2.0 Reading Sample Questions 3 with all his might—just as though he were flying—he moved the tiniest bit toward shore.

As the young bird splashed his wings in the water, bright sparkling droplets showered on his head. The drops spilled over his back and soaked his last dry feathers.

The pond looked calm and quiet. But the baby blackbird wasn't the only animal in the water. And some of the creatures—big fish, bullfrogs, and snapping turtles—would eat little birds whenever they had the chance.

As the little bird struggled along toward shore, a female bass noticed the ripples he was making. Then the big fish saw tiny feet and wet, feathery wing tips coming toward her. She started to drift upward toward the struggling bird.

Meanwhile, the bird's frantic parents were watching from the willow tree. They shrieked and screamed and darted about in the branches while the young bird swam on. By now the little bird's wet feathers felt very heavy, and he was getting tired. He swam slower and slower. All the while, the bass kept moving toward him. With one more powerful

3 FCAT 2.0 Reading Sample Questions swish of her tail and a snap of her jaws, the wet blackbird would be hers—feet, feathers, and all!

But just as the bass was about to lunge for the bird, an otter came streaking through the water. The fish zipped away from the hungry otter and went to find cover in the weeds. Off went the otter to search for the bass. So the little bird was safe from the fish! With a last push of his wing tips, the young blackbird reached the edge of the pond. He flapped out of the water and crawled up on shore. There he dropped onto the damp clay soil in a wet heap of feathers. Now his parents circled wildly above him, squawking and shrieking. With luck, their noise would frighten away any enemies. As the young bird lay there, the rays of the summer sun warmed and dried him. He stood up and began to fluff out his feathers and straighten them with his beak.

Then he stretched his wings and gave a little push with his feet against the damp clay of the shore. Off he flew into a clump of cattails growing on the other side of the pond.

For the rest of that day the little bird rested in the shelter of the cattails. Meanwhile his parents still clamored and fussed. But now they also brought him all the insects he could eat. The next morning, the young bird flew away from the pond and headed for a marsh. There were plenty of dangers in the marsh, as he would soon discover. But for this day, at least, he would stay away from the pond.

AnswerA: First they are calm; then they are anxious.
AnswerB: First they are peaceful; then they are restless.
AnswerC: First they are protective; then they are relaxed.
AnswerD: First they are nervous; then they are frightened.

Where Surnames Come From
Most people have a first name and a family name, or surname. Long ago, many people had only one name. As villages grew bigger, there might be five men called John! People needed a way to tell them apart, so surnames began.
Some surnames came from jobs. A smith worked with metal, so a man who made horseshoes might be called John Smith. A baker baked bread, and a cooper made wooden barrels.
Other surnames came from places. Someone who lived near a hill might be called Hill, and someone who lived beside a brook, or small stream, might become Brook.
Many surnames simply mean 'son of'. Johnson was once John's son, and Peterson was Peter's son.
Today, children usually share a surname with one or both parents, so the name passes down through the family. Some families join two surnames with a hyphen.
Next time you hear a surname, think about the story it might tell!

Roads That Lasted
About two thousand years ago, the ancient Romans built one of the greatest road systems in history. Their roads stretched across Europe, North Africa and the Middle East.
Roman roads were built in layers, a bit like a giant sandwich. Workers first dug a deep trench. They filled the bottom with large stones, then added smaller stones and gravel. On top, they fitted flat paving stones tightly together.
The roads were also slightly curved, higher in the middle than at the edges. When it rained, the water ran off into ditches at the sides. This stopped puddles from forming and kept the road strong.
Roman builders liked their roads to be as straight as possible. That way, soldiers, traders and messengers could travel quickly from town to town. Along the way, tall stone markers called milestones showed how far it was to the next town.
Amazingly, some Roman roads are still used today.

Drawing with Scissors
Henri Matisse was a French artist famous for his bold, bright paintings. He loved colour more than almost anything else.
In 1941, when Matisse was seventy-one, he became very ill and needed a big operation. Afterwards, he was too weak to stand at an easel for long. He spent much of his time in bed or in a wheelchair. Many people thought his life as an artist was over.
Matisse did not give up. He asked his helpers to paint large sheets of paper in brilliant colours. Then, holding a big pair of scissors, he cut out shapes such as leaves, stars, birds and swirling seaweed. His helpers pinned the shapes to the walls while Matisse told them exactly where each piece should go.
He called this 'drawing with scissors'. Some of his cut-outs grew so large that they covered whole walls. Today, these joyful works hang in famous galleries around the world, and many people think they are among his very best.

AnswerC: his wheelchair and bed
AnswerD: pictures of seaweed
